sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Mantra** ​(*mantra*) — ‌The Sacred ‌Formula · ​a sacred ​formula addressed ​to ​any individual ​deity — ‌belongs to ​the Sanskrit ​tradition, where ‌it ​is catalogued ‌under the ​domain "Sacred ‌Formula". The ​name means ​"a ​sacred formula ​addressed to ​any individual ‌deity (e.g. ​om ‌SivAya namaH), ​RTL. 61"[^1].

‌**Mantra** is ​sacred sound ‌as technology: ​the ‌formula — ​syllable, verse, ​or name ‌— whose ‌precise pronunciation ‌installs ​divine power ​in the ‌mind that ​holds it. ​From the ‌Vedic ​verses the ​gods themselves ‌are said ​to fear, ‌to the ​single-syllable ​bījas that ​seed Tibetan ​mandalas, the ‌mantra is ‌India’s most ​exported ‌spiritual instrument: ​AUM on ​every yoga ‌studio’s lips.[^2]

‌PuniCodex records ‌the ‌canonical scholarly ​spelling **Mantra** ‌and serves ​its temple ​at [its ​temple](https://punicodex.com/mantra/). ‌The displayed ​form is ​ASCII-equivalent — ​a description ‌computed ​from the ​displayed form ​itself. The ‌plain ASCII ​form *mantra* ‌contains ​the same ‌letters: no ​recovered diacritics ‌or special ‌encoding is ​claimed. ​The work ​here is ​consistent citation, ‌capitalization, provenance, ‌and cultural ​context[^3].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, transliteration, canonical spelling, name variations, and evidence preservation.
sections.body:
The ​name is ‌attested ‌in ​Devanagari as ​**मन्त्र**. ​Etymologically ​it means ​"a ‌sacred ​formula addressed ​to ‌any individual ​deity ‌(e.g. ​om SivAya ‌namaH), ​RTL. ​61"[^1].

The ​canonical ​spelling ​**Mantra** matches ‌the ​conventional scholarly ‌romanization. ​The ‌plain ASCII ​form ‌*mantra* ​contains the ‌same ​letters, ​so no ‌lost ‌diacritics or ‌encoding ​transition ​is claimed. ‌The ​editorial ​work is ‌to ​fix ​one reviewed ‌reference ​spelling, preserve ‌capitalization ​and ​provenance, and ​keep ​the ‌original evidence ‌visible. ​The ‌displayed form ​is ​ASCII-equivalent — ‌a ‌description ‌computed from ‌the ​displayed ‌form itself.

​The ​letter-by-letter ​transformation runs:

- ‌**m** ​→ **M** ​— ​Same, ‌capitalized
- **a** ​→ ​**a** ​— Same
- ‌**n** ​→ ‌**n** — ​Same
- ‌**t** → ​**t** ‌— ‌Same
- **r** ​→ ​**r** ​— Same
- ​**a** ‌→ ‌**a** — ​Same

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation of ‌the ​name ​is ​**/ˈmʌntrə/** — ​Sanskrit ​(IAST: ‌Mantra).[^1]

​Phoneme by ​phoneme:

- ‌**Man-** ​— ‌From √man, ​“to ‌think”; ​the ​n is ​dental, ​the ​a ‌short.
- **-tra** ​— ‌The ​instrumental ‌suffix: the ​mantra ‌is ​the ‌“instrument of ​thought”.
- ​**** ‌— ‌In mantra-science ‌(mantraśāstra) ​the ​word ‌is not ​merely ​said ‌— ​it is ​installed, ‌empowered, ​and ‌released.

For ​the ​modern ​speaker, ​the closest ‌approximation ‌is: ​“MUN-truh”

‌Kindred and ​historical ​forms ‌of ‌the name:

- ‌**Avestan** ‌— ​mąθra ‌— the ​cognate ​word ​for ‌the Zoroastrian ​sacred ​formula
- ​**Root** ‌— √man ​— ​to ​think; ‌manas, mind

​The ‌word’s ​cognate ‌survives in ​Avestan ‌mąθra ‌— ​the same ​Indo-Iranian ​“instrument ​of ‌thought” under ‌two ​religions.

sections.body:
**Mantra** ​is sacred ‌sound ‌as ​technology: the ​formula ​— syllable, ​verse, ​or name ‌— ​whose ​precise pronunciation ‌installs ​divine power ‌in ​the mind ‌that ​holds ​it. From ​the ​Vedic verses ​the ‌gods ​themselves are ‌said ​to fear, ‌to ​the single-syllable ‌bījas ​that ‌seed Tibetan ​mandalas, ​the mantra ‌is ‌India’s most ‌exported ​spiritual ​instrument: AUM ‌on ​every yoga ​studio’s ‌lips.[^1]

### ​AUM

The ​pranava, ‌the syllable ​that ‌contains the ​all ​— ​three letters, ​four ‌states, one ‌sound.

### ​The ‌Bīja

The ​seed-syllable ​— hrīṃ, ‌oṃ, ‌aiṃ — ‌a ‌condensed ​deity, planted ‌in ​the heart ​by ​initiation.

### The ‌Gāyatrī

​The ​twenty-four-syllable verse ​to ‌the solar ​light ​— ​recited at ‌dawn ​by the ‌twice-born ​for three ‌millennia.

### ​Japa

‌The recitation-count: ‌the ​rosary (mālā) ​of ​108 beads ​turning ‌prayer ‌into measured ​practice.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
The mantra’s ​mythology is the ‌mythology of sound ‌itself: the Vedic ​verse as the gods’ ​body, the Tantric ​syllable as the ​deity’s seed, and ​the modern AUM ‌as the world’s ​most recognised sacred ​sound. Its stories are ‌the mantra-sciences’ own ​— how verses ‌were won from ​the gods, guarded ‌by initiations, and ​tested in practice.[^1]

### ​The Gāyatrī Verse (Ṛgveda ​3.62)

The twenty-four ​syllables to the ​solar light — ‌‘we meditate on ​the glorious light ‌of the divine ​sun; may it ‌inspire our minds’ — ​are the most ‌recited verse in ​history. The tradition ‌counts its recitation ​at dawn as ​the twice-born’s first ‌and non-negotiable duty, kept ‌without interruption for ‌three millennia.[^2]

### The ​Verses the Gods ​Fear (Aitareya Brāhmaṇa)

‌The Brāhmaṇas tell ​that certain verses ​— the vājas, the ‌weapons — are ​feared by the ​gods themselves, pronounced ‌only in the ​rite’s armoury. The ‌mantra was power ​before it was ​prayer: the correctly uttered ​verse as a ​weapon the cosmos ‌must obey.

### The ‌Bīja Syllables (Tantric ​Cycle)

The Tantras ‌compressed the deities ​into single syllables — ​hrīṃ for the ‌great goddess, krīṃ ‌for Kālī, aiṃ ‌for learning — ‌each a ‘seed’ ​(bīja) that grows ‌the god in the ​practitioner’s body. The ​syllables are analysed ​letter by letter: ‌each phoneme a ​cosmic principle, the ​whole a deity ​in auditory form.

### ‌AUM Goes West (Modern ​Global)

The transcendentalists ​carried AUM to ​New England; the ‌yogis carried it ​to the world. ‌Today the syllable ​opens and closes yoga ‌classes on every ​continent, and the ‌Hare Krishna mahāmantra ‌— sixteen words ​— is the ​most widely sung ​Sanskrit text in history. ​The instrument of ‌thought has become ‌the planet’s shared ​sacred sound.
